editorial:
You follow Antoine, a young Parisian boy who keeps getting let down by the adults around him. His parents are cold, teachers are harsh, and even small mistakes turn into big trouble. He spends time with his best friend Rene, dreaming of freedom and a better life. The movie feels honest and sad, but also warm when the boys share small moments. You feel every unfair moment because Antoine is just a kid trying to survive in a tough world.

The acting feels natural, especially the young lead, and the black-and-white streets of Paris give the story a real, lived-in feel. The pacing is slow but steady, so you need patience, and some scenes may feel heavy. Still, it is a powerful coming-of-age story for viewers who like character-driven drama.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, Antoine escapes from the detention center and runs toward the ocean. He reaches the beach and keeps running until he hits the water, then turns back toward the camera. The movie freezes on his face, leaving you with a mix of freedom and uncertainty. It does not give a neat answer, but it shows how trapped he still feels.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves classic coming-of-age dramas.
